title: Integrating Quotients Containing Trigonometric Functions Using Substitution

sections.normalized_html:
Notice that the numerator is proportional to the derivative of the denominator, because

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(1+\tan^2 x) = 2\tan{x}\sec^2 x.]

So, let [MATH: u = 1+\tan^2 x.] Differentiating, we have

[MATH: \dfrac{\textrm{d} u}{\textrm{d}x } = 2\tan x\sec^2 x \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac 1 2 \textrm d u = \tan x\sec^2 x\,\textrm d x.]

Calculating the limits for [MATH: u] gives

[MATH: x]

[MATH: 0]

[MATH: \pi/4]

[MATH: u]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: 2]

We now substitute and evaluate, as follows:

[MATH: ∫_{0}^{π/4}(\tan x\sec^{2} x)/(1 + \tan^{2} x)dx|= ∫_{0}^{π/4}(1)/(1 + \tan^{2} x) ⋅ \tan x\sec^{2} xdx; = ∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(u) ⋅ (1)/(2)du; = (1)/(2)∫_{1}^{2}(1)/(u)du; = (1)/(2)(\ln 2 − \ln 1); = (1)/(2)\ln 2]
